opus-5.5.text:
For me, finding a research idea is rarely a single "eureka" moment. It's more like a slow accumulation of discomfort. You read papers, you run experiments, you talk to people, and at some point something just doesn't sit right with you. Maybe everyone is accepting an assumption that seems a bit arbitrary, or there's a result that people treat as settled but you feel it hasn't really been understood. That small feeling of "wait, why is it like this?" is usually where a good idea starts.

I often tell my students that the idea itself isn't the scarce resource. Ideas are cheap; everyone has dozens. What matters is taste, being able to judge which questions are worth spending a year or two of your life on. For that, I ask myself a few things. First, if this works, will it change how people think, or will it just add one more line to a table? Second, is it the right time? Some ideas are great but ten years too early, because the compute, the data, or the tools aren't there yet. Third, do I have some unique angle on it? If a hundred other groups could do exactly the same thing next week, it's probably not the best use of my time.

I also think you have to be willing to go a bit against the current. In our field, especially in the last few years, there's a strong pull toward whatever is hot at the moment. Everyone piles into the same direction, and the marginal value of one more paper there gets small. Some of the work I'm proudest of came from stepping back and revisiting things people considered "old" or "solved." For example, asking whether a simple, classic design can still compete if you modernize it carefully. Those questions sound unglamorous, but they often reveal that what we believed was progress was partly about training recipes or scale rather than the core idea.

Another part is that research ideas come from doing, not just thinking. You can't sit in a room and wait for inspiration. You get your hands dirty, you build things, you look at failure cases, you visualize what the model actually learned. A lot of the time the real question only becomes clear halfway through the project, and the paper you end up writing is quite different from the one you planned. I think you have to stay open to that and not be too attached to your initial hypothesis.

Finally, I care a lot about whether the idea is something I'm genuinely curious about. Research is long and full of frustration. If you're only chasing a publication or a benchmark number, it's very hard to sustain. But if there's a question you really want to know the answer to, even if nobody else cares yet, that curiosity carries you through the hard parts. And honestly, those are often the projects that end up mattering most.

r001.rationale: The response discusses crowding around popular research directions and choosing projects worth a year or two, but it does not suggest competitive pressure limits a research cycle to six months or less.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think most people get this backwards. They imagine there's a moment where an idea arrives, and then the work begins. For me it's almost the opposite: the idea is usually the last thing that shows up, and it only shows up because I've been living inside a problem long enough that something starts to feel wrong.

That feeling of "something is wrong here" is really the whole thing. When I was working on ConvNeXt, the starting point wasn't "let's build a better ConvNet." It was more like an itch. Everyone was saying transformers had won in vision, and the explanation was always about attention, about the architecture being fundamentally superior. But when I actually looked at the comparisons, the training recipes were completely different. The ConvNets were being evaluated with 2015 recipes and the transformers with 2021 recipes. So the question wasn't an idea yet, it was just a discomfort: are we sure we're measuring what we think we're measuring? The paper came out of chasing that discomfort honestly, step by step, without deciding the answer in advance.

So one principle I try to hold onto is: find the thing the field believes without having really checked. Those are usually hiding in plain sight. Nobody is deliberately hiding them, it's just that once a narrative forms, people stop testing it. Students often think they need to be in some exotic corner of the literature to find a gap. In my experience the biggest gaps are right in the middle of the most popular topic, in the assumptions everyone is making.

The second thing is taste, and I know that sounds vague. What I mean is being able to tell the difference between a problem that's interesting and a problem that's important. There are many interesting problems that don't matter. A good test for me is: if this works, does it change how people do things afterward? Or does it just produce a number on a benchmark? I try to spend most of my time on the first kind, even though the second kind is much easier to publish.

And third, I'd say ideas come from doing, not from thinking. I'm a bit skeptical of sitting in a room trying to have an idea. Most of my good ideas came from running experiments that failed in a way I didn't expect. The failure is the information. When you read a paper and something doesn't add up, when you re-implement something and can't reproduce it, when you ablate a component and the result goes the wrong direction, that's where the real research starts. So I tell my students: don't wait for the idea. Pick a question you genuinely care about, get your hands dirty, and pay very close attention to the moments when you're surprised. The idea will find you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how research ideas emerge through sustained work and experimentation, but it does not mention competitive pressure or suggest a research cycle of at most six months.

astra-6.text:
I think finding a research idea is less about sitting down and trying to invent something, and more about developing a sense of what doesn’t quite make sense to you. You read a paper, run an experiment, or look at a result, and something conflicts with your intuition. That gap can be a starting point.

The important thing is to make the question concrete. If you think a particular component is necessary, what happens when you remove it? If one approach works better, is it really for the reason people give? A small, well-controlled experiment can be much more useful than a very elaborate proposal.

And I think the process is iterative. You don’t necessarily start with the question that eventually appears in the paper. You start with something vague, get a surprising result, and gradually understand what the actual question is. So I would focus less on finding a perfect idea upfront and more on building a loop where you can test your intuition and learn from what happens.

r001.rationale: The response describes an iterative process of testing ideas, but does not mention competitive pressure or a research cycle limited to six months.

sol-6.1.text:
I think finding a research idea is less about sitting down and trying to invent something, and more about developing a sense of what is interesting. Often it starts with something you don’t understand: Why does this work? Why does this seemingly reasonable approach fail? Is this complexity actually necessary?

Then you need to spend time with that question. Read related work, run some small experiments, and see whether your intuition survives. A lot of ideas sound exciting until you test them. But sometimes an unexpected result gives you a much better question than the one you started with.

So for me, it’s an iterative process. You need curiosity to get started, but you also need judgment—and that judgment develops through doing research, including pursuing ideas that don’t work out. I wouldn’t wait for a perfect idea before getting my hands dirty.

r001.rationale: The response describes idea development as iterative but does not mention competitive pressure or a research cycle limited to six months.
